summary: This is a position paper giving the author's personal views on how quality of service should fit into Information-Centric Networking protocols such as CCNx or NDN. It argues these need an approach different from TCP/IP, proposes design patterns for classification and differentiated treatment, and considers caches as resources. It is not an ICNRG product.

plainLanguage.summary: In a network that fetches things by name, sending a quick reply to the important requests needs new ideas. This is one author's opinion on how to give some requests priority.

questions: how does caching affect quality of service
interest table in named data networking
subtitle: Adapting quality of service to Information-Centric Networking's unique architecture.

tldr.problem: Information-Centric Networking protocols like CCNx and NDN are fundamentally different from TCP/IP: they use names instead of addresses, stateful hop-by-hop forwarding, and built-in caches. Traditional IP quality-of-service approaches like Diffserv and Intserv do not fit well.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9064 is a position paper proposing QoS principles tailored to ICN: use hierarchical names for traffic classification, put consumers in control of resource allocation via Interest messages, let producers influence cache decisions, and allow network operators to match customer SLAs to cache availability. It outlines design patterns and architectural considerations without specifying a complete protocol.
tldr.outcome: The paper provides guidance for future ICN QoS specifications and demonstrates that ICN's design allows richer QoS capabilities than IP at potentially lower overhead, especially for multipath and cached content delivery.

facts.label: ICN core resources
facts.value: Link bandwidth, CS cache, PIT memory, CPU

today: RFC 9064 is an Informational position paper published in June 2021 by an IRTF member. It represents the author's personal views, not a consensus position, but has the support of the Information-Centric Networking Research Group. It has not been updated or superseded and continues to guide research into ICN QoS mechanisms.

sections.title: Why ICN Needs Different QoS
sections.content:
Information-Centric Networking (ICN) is a different philosophy from TCP/IP. Instead of asking for data from a specific address, you ask by name: "Give me the latest news video." The network routes your request hop by hop through routers, and the first router that has a cached copy sends it back. This is powerful for content distribution and resilience but demands a different approach to quality of service.

TCP/IP's Diffserv and Intserv approaches rely on classifying traffic by IP addresses and port numbers. In ICN, there are no IP addresses—only hierarchical names. Also, ICN routers maintain state (a Pending Interest Table tracks outstanding requests) and cache content, creating new resources to allocate: the PIT memory, the Content Store cache, forwarding CPU, and link bandwidth.

This position paper is the author's personal views on how QoS should work in ICN protocols. It advocates designing QoS from scratch for ICN rather than copying IP mechanisms. The paper proposes architectural principles but not a complete protocol specification.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP/IP calls things by address: "Send to 192.0.2.1." ICN calls things by name: "Send me the movie." When you change what you're asking for, you need to change how you control which requests get priority.

sections.title: ICN Basics and Congestion Control
sections.content:
In ICN, a consumer sends an Interest message asking for content by hierarchical name. Routers (called forwarders) forward it hop by hop, keeping state in a Pending Interest Table (PIT) so they know where to send the answer. When a producer or a forwarder's cache has the content, it sends back a Data message on the reverse path.

Forwarders can also act as caches, storing Data messages in a Content Store (CS). Future Interests for the same content are satisfied from the cache, never reaching the producer. This is why caching is central to ICN's power but also why cache resource allocation matters for QoS.

ICN supports hop-by-hop congestion control rather than just end-to-end control as in TCP. Each forwarder can decide how many Interests to accept and forward, based on available bandwidth on the return path. This allows faster feedback and potentially better resource use than waiting for the consumer to reduce its sending rate.
sections.plainLanguage: In ICN, you send a request upstream until someone has the answer. They send it back down the same path. Along the way, routers can save a copy so the next request for the same thing gets answered faster. They can also control the flow of requests to match the available bandwidth.

sections.title: What Resources Can We Allocate?
sections.content:
QoS is about deciding which traffic gets what share of limited resources. In ICN forwarders, the main resources are:

Link bandwidth: packets waiting in output queues.

Content Store (CS) capacity: space for caching content.

Forwarder memory: the Pending Interest Table (PIT) can grow huge in high-traffic, long-RTT scenarios.

Compute capacity: CPU for forwarding decisions and name-prefix lookups.

IP has only link bandwidth and CPU. ICN adds two new resources—CS and PIT—that demand explicit allocation for good QoS. The number of equivalence classes (flows) a forwarder can track is limited by memory and compute. Operators must balance fine-grained per-flow control against the cost of tracking many flows.
sections.plainLanguage: The network has pipes (links), memory for saved copies, memory for tracking outstanding requests, and CPU. All of these can get congested. Good QoS means sharing them fairly or unfairly by policy.

sections.title: Where ICN's Design Helps QoS
sections.content:
Hierarchical names are richer than IP 5-tuples for classification. A name like /video/news/today/1080p expresses both content type and structure. QoS rules can naturally match name prefixes and hierarchies. An application can group related content together for shared treatment.

Symmetric routing in ICN means a request goes one way and the answer comes back the same way. IP suffers from asymmetric routing (forward and reverse paths differ), complicating QoS. ICN avoids this.

Stateful forwarding with the PIT means state exists only while traffic is active. QoS state can be created on-demand and cleaned up automatically. IP's Intserv requires per-flow signaling to create and maintain state.

Single forwarding semantic simplifies matters. IP has unicast, anycast, and multicast, each with different QoS needs. ICN has one model that works uniformly for single source or multiple sources.

Hop-by-hop control** lets consumers influence resource allocation per-Interest rather than waiting for end-to-end feedback. This can make congestion control more responsive.

Caching is built in and can be leveraged for QoS. Producers and consumers can influence what gets cached and for how long, using QoS treatments to match cache behavior to application needs.
sections.plainLanguage: ICN has some built-in advantages: names tell you what the content is, the answer always comes back the way the request went, state appears and disappears automatically, and requests can be stopped early if a cache has what you need.

sections.title: Principles for ICN QoS
sections.content:
Based on the differences and advantages, the author proposes five key principles for ICN QoS design:

1. Use name hierarchies for traffic classification. Define equivalence classes of traffic directly from content names rather than creating a separate traffic classification system. This keeps QoS aligned with application semantics.

2. Let consumers control link and forwarding resource allocation. Base all resource allocation decisions on the arrival of Interest messages. Consumers implicitly grant permission to use bandwidth and memory when they send an Interest. This is more efficient than reserving resources in advance and avoids wasting bandwidth on data the consumer will drop.

3. Let producers influence cache allocation. Producers know their content's lifetime and popularity. They should control via cache directives (already in CCNx and NDN) whether data is worth caching and for how long. Network operators then map producer policies to physical cache space.

4. Give consumers indirect influence over caching. Consumers can request QoS treatments that guide caching decisions, such as "prefer caching for robustness" or "do not cache, I need fresh data."

5. Let network operators map QoS to physical resources. Operators decide how much cache space is reserved for each equivalence class or how hard individual objects are fought for in eviction policies. They bridge producer policies, consumer requests, and available cache space.
sections.plainLanguage: Five rules for designing QoS in ICN: use the content name to decide priority, let the person asking decide which requests get bandwidth, let the content owner say how long to remember it, let the asker influence that indirectly, and let the operator set the final rules based on what they have available.

sections.title: New QoS Treatments for ICN
sections.content:
Traditional Diffserv classes (best-effort, assured forwarding, expedited forwarding) apply to IP but do not capture ICN's possibilities. The paper proposes new QoS treatment types that leverage ICN's unique features:

Burst treatment: An Interest says "I want to request a large amount of data; reserve bandwidth for N Data packets in a row." The forwarder allocates resources upfront or rejects the burst if unavailable.

Reliable treatment: Prioritize PIT and cache space to ensure delivery even in constrained environments. Useful for critical IoT sensors.

Search treatment: Try many paths or many sources in parallel or serially to maximize the probability of finding content. Trade higher bandwidth for higher success rate.

These treatments are impossible in IP because IP has no built-in caching, symmetric routing, or per-packet state. ICN enables them naturally.

The author notes that richer treatments like Intserv's TSPEC (traffic specification with bandwidth and delay guarantees) could be adapted for ICN but would face challenges with multi-destination forwarding and admission control.
sections.plainLanguage: In IP, quality of service mostly means "prioritize this" or "do your best." In ICN, you can say things like "try lots of sources" or "cache aggressively" because the network remembers things and takes different paths.
